item.statement: Cocaine cancels out alcohol, so someone who has had both isn't really drunk any more.
item.why: In small lab studies, known second-hand from one review, people felt only a little less drunk or no different, and blood alcohol stayed the same or was about a tenth lower. Nobody tested driving, and about 4 in 100 drivers who died in crashes had both drugs in their blood.

lines.short: People given cocaine with alcohol did not feel more drunk, and sometimes slightly less.
lines.but: This is second-hand from one review of small studies, and no one tested driving.
how: A review gathered 14 small laboratory studies. The four that asked how drunk people felt had 8 to 11 people each. Those studies have not been read here, so the figures are second-hand.
In three of the four, people said they felt a little less drunk with cocaine; in one, nothing changed. Two of the three falls were too small to be clear.
Cocaine also made some alcohol-affected test scores less poor, and blood alcohol stayed the same or was about 10 percent lower.

Nobody asked other people how drunk someone looked, and no study tested driving. Of drivers who died in crashes, about 4 in 100 had both drugs in their blood, so the mix did not protect them from alcohol's effects.

item.statement: Someone overdosing on meth goes quiet and sleepy, with slow breathing.
item.why: It can look like a body in overdrive: a racing heart, fast breathing, a very hot body, and a person who is very restless and upset. Some lose touch with reality, though how often each sign shows up varies a lot.

lines.short: A meth overdose can look like a body in overdrive. The heart races, breathing speeds up, and people get very restless and upset. Some lose touch with reality.
lines.but: That's second-hand, from two reviews of hospital studies, and how often each sign shows up varies a lot.
how: Signs include a racing heart, high blood pressure, fast breathing and wide pupils. People can be very restless and upset.
The body can get very hot. Chest pain and organ failure can happen, and some people die.
One review found psychosis (losing touch with reality) in 12 to 80 in 100 people seen in hospital. Suicidal thoughts or acts showed up in 6 to 50, depending on the study.
Neither review says how many patients die.

item.statement: People who try weed are more likely to get hooked than people who try alcohol.
item.why: In an older US survey, about 9 in 100 people who had ever tried cannabis had been dependent at some point: fewer than for alcohol, tobacco, cocaine or heroin. Newer US figures are higher, but they count milder cases and only people who used in the past year.

lines.short: About 9 in 100 people who ever tried it, in two older US surveys.
lines.but: The surveys are from 1990 to 2005 and used a narrower definition than today's.
how: A US survey in 1990 to 1992 asked about 8,000 people aged 15 to 54 about drug use and dependence.
Of those who had ever used cannabis, even once, about 9 in 100 had been dependent at some point: fewer than for tobacco, heroin, cocaine or alcohol.
A second US survey, in 2001 to 2005, estimated about 9 in 100 over a lifetime; half of those who became dependent did so within about 5 years of first use.
Newer US figures are higher, about 3 in 10, but they count milder cases and only people who used in the past year.

item.statement: A positive urine test for weed shows the person used it in the past few days.
item.why: THC is stored in body fat and leaves it slowly: in two people who had used heavily, urine tests found cannabis for 67 and 93 days. A positive test doesn't show when or how much someone used.

lines.short: Smoked, THC peaks in the blood within minutes; eaten, it rises slowly over hours.
lines.but: Old, small lab studies of weak cannabis, described in one review.
how: After smoking, THC in the blood peaked within minutes and fell to low levels within 2 hours.
After eating, it peaked 1 to 6 hours later, at lower levels, and the effects started later and lasted longer.
THC is stored in body fat and leaves it slowly; in people who use often, it can be found for days to weeks.

After one cigarette the last positive urine test came about 1 to 4 days later on average, and cannabis was found for 67 and 93 days in two people who used heavily; a positive test does not show when or how much.

item.statement: Among people who say a trip changed their beliefs, most afterwards thought plants could be conscious.
item.why: In a survey of 1,606 such people, 26 in 100 recalled thinking so before the trip and 61 in 100 after. They were looking back about 8 years on average, and superstitions, like black cats bringing bad luck, didn't rise.

lines.short: These studies can't say if it's the truth. But after a retreat, beliefs shifted a bit, towards ideas like other worlds and a conscious universe. The shift was still there 6 months later.
lines.but: The main study had no comparison group, and only 122 of over 800 people answered every survey. Most already leaned that way.
how: People answered questions a week before a psychedelic retreat or ceremony, then 4 weeks and 6 months after. In the 122 who answered all three, belief in things like other worlds rose a little.
First-timers shifted more. In one exploratory analysis, the shift went with feeling in tune with the group, not clearly with how mystical or visual the trip felt.
In a trial in depression, beliefs shifted after psilocybin. They shifted a little after a standard antidepressant too, and the gap was too small to be sure of.

A survey asked 1,606 people who said a trip had changed their beliefs to look back, about 8 years on average. 26 in 100 recalled thinking plants could be conscious before, and 61 in 100 after. Superstitions, like black cats bringing bad luck, didn't rise.

item.statement: In 2001 Portugal made it legal to have drugs for your own use.
item.why: Not legal: having any drug for your own use became an offence handled by regional panels instead of a crime. Mostly for that reason, crime arrests for drugs fell from over 14,000 to between 5,000 and 5,500 a year.

lines.short: Mixed. Adults who'd ever tried a drug went from 8 to 12 in 100, but use in the last year barely moved. New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell.
lines.but: Treatment and other help grew too, starting in 1999, so these figures can't show what the law alone did.
how: In 2001, having any drug for your own use became an offence handled by regional panels, not a crime. Mostly for that reason, crime arrests for drugs fell from over 14,000 to 5,000–5,500 a year.
Adults who had ever tried an illegal drug rose from about 8 to 12 in 100 (2001 to 2007); past-year use barely changed.
New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell from 907 (2000) to 267 (2008). The paper says this has been credited mainly to more harm reduction services, without saying by whom.
Deaths doctors judged drug-caused fell from about 76 to 20 (2001 to 2008). Deaths with drugs found fell, then rose as testing more than doubled.

item.statement: After Portugal decriminalised drugs in 2001, the share of adults using drugs in the past year barely changed.
item.why: Adults who had ever tried an illegal drug rose from about 8 to 12 in 100, but past-year use barely moved. Treatment and other help grew at the same time, so these figures can't show what the law alone did.

lines.short: Mixed. Adults who'd ever tried a drug went from 8 to 12 in 100, but use in the last year barely moved. New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell.
lines.but: Treatment and other help grew too, starting in 1999, so these figures can't show what the law alone did.
how: In 2001, having any drug for your own use became an offence handled by regional panels, not a crime. Mostly for that reason, crime arrests for drugs fell from over 14,000 to 5,000–5,500 a year.
Adults who had ever tried an illegal drug rose from about 8 to 12 in 100 (2001 to 2007); past-year use barely changed.
New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell from 907 (2000) to 267 (2008). The paper says this has been credited mainly to more harm reduction services, without saying by whom.
Deaths doctors judged drug-caused fell from about 76 to 20 (2001 to 2008). Deaths with drugs found fell, then rose as testing more than doubled.

item.statement: MDMA with therapy has helped people with PTSD more than the same therapy with a dummy pill.
item.why: In two trials, 61 to 70 in 100 no longer had PTSD after MDMA, against 27 to 39 in 100 after a dummy pill. But in the trial that asked, most people knew which pill they'd had, so expectations may explain part of the gap.

lines.short: Yes, in two trials. With the same therapy, 61 to 70 in 100 no longer had PTSD after MDMA, against 27 to 39 in 100 after a dummy pill.
lines.but: In the trial that asked, most knew which pill they'd had, so expectations may explain part of the gap.
how: In two trials run for one sponsor, 194 adults with PTSD had up to three long sessions with MDMA or a dummy pill, plus the same therapy.
Both groups improved a lot. About 4 months later, PTSD scores had dropped about 9 to 12 points more with MDMA, on a scale of 0 to 80.
Counting everyone who started, 61 to 70 in 100 on MDMA no longer had PTSD at about 4 months, against 27 to 39 in 100 on the dummy pill.
Neither trial reports measuring what people expected. The trials report nothing after 4 months, and none we read compared MDMA-assisted therapy with a trauma-focused talking therapy.

item.statement: In the days after a psychedelic like LSD or shrooms, people usually feel lower than before, like a comedown.
item.why: In most studies that checked, people reported less low mood and stress and more wellbeing a day to a month after, and none found mental health worse on average. Most were supported sessions with no dummy-pill group, so nobody knows the cause.

lines.short: Often better than before: less low mood and stress, more wellbeing, in most studies that checked. Some people got headaches, usually for a day or two, or slept badly.
lines.but: Most studies had no blind dummy-pill group, so nobody knows the cause, and most were supported sessions, not recreational use.
how: A review gathered 48 studies of psilocybin, ayahuasca, LSD, 5-MeO-DMT and mescaline, with 1,774 people in all. People answered the same questionnaires before, and again a day to a month after.
Most studies that checked (70 to 90 in 100) found less depression and stress, and more wellbeing, mindfulness and closeness to others. None found mental health worse on average.
Of 25 studies that said they looked for problems, 14 found some: mostly headaches (52 people, usually lasting a day or two), then poor sleep, tension and exhaustion.
One person had severe anxiety, and one went back to using methamphetamine. Half the studies didn't say whether they looked for problems at all.

item.statement: Stopping benzos such as Xanax or Valium suddenly can bring on seizures.
item.why: Two expert reviews warn that seizures after stopping suddenly can be life-threatening. They don't say how often: the only count they give is 2 of 11 prisoners on very high doses, in 1961.

lines.short: It can be: two expert reviews warn of life-threatening seizures, but not how often. The only count they give is 2 of 11 prisoners on very high doses, in 1961.
lines.but: These are expert reviews, not studies. Their seizure warnings give no rates, and one gives no source for them.
how: One review says withdrawal symptoms can follow 4 to 6 weeks of use, in about 15 to 30 in 100 people. That figure comes from the author's own earlier paper.

Symptoms listed include anxiety, poor sleep, aches, tingling and sensitivity to light and sound, and can feel like the problem the pills were for. Sleeping pills stopped after even a few nights can bring back worse sleep for a while.

Both warn that seizures after stopping suddenly can be life-threatening. One says severe reactions can also happen when cutting down slowly, and that many reports are anecdotes; the other gives no source for its warning.
The only count comes second-hand, from a 1961 study: 11 prisoners who had taken very high doses for months were switched to a dummy pill. Ten had withdrawal, and 2 had seizures.

item.statement: In a lab test, people who often have caffeine were sleepier and slower without it than people who rarely do.
item.why: Skipping caffeine left them the sleepiest and slowest, and taking it only brought them level with people who rarely have it, no higher. People chose their own caffeine habits, so something else about them could explain it.

lines.short: In one lab study, caffeine made everyone faster. But those who often have it only got as alert as those who rarely do.
lines.but: Only one study, and people chose their own caffeine habits, so something else about them could explain it.
how: In Bristol, UK, 416 adults were asked to skip caffeine overnight. The next day, chance decided who got caffeine pills and who got dummy pills.
By the afternoon, people who often have caffeine but got dummy pills were the sleepiest and slowest. They made the most mistakes.
Caffeine brought them about level with people who rarely have it, no higher. In those people, caffeine raised jitters, not alertness.
Five people who often have caffeine quit the test day early. All five had dummy pills; four gave headache and feeling sick as reasons.

item.statement: Most people who die of a heroin overdose have no other drug in their body.
item.why: In older studies, no other drug was found in only 23 to 48 in 100 deaths labelled heroin overdose, and alcohol was found in 29 to 75 in 100. Finding a drug doesn't show it caused the death.

lines.short: Not necessarily. Older studies often found other drugs too: alcohol in 29 to 75 in 100 of these deaths. But finding a drug doesn't show it caused the death.
lines.but: These old records cannot tell how many deaths heroin alone caused.
how: In older studies from the USA, Australia and Europe, morphine was the only drug found in 23 to 48 in 100 deaths labelled heroin overdose. Alcohol was found in 29 to 75 in 100.
Many deaths took hours, and other people were often there: more than half the time, in four studies. These come second-hand, from a review.

In England and Wales in 2000, researchers classed 23 in 100 accidental drug-related deaths reported by coroners as something other than a direct overdose, like an infection, an injury, or drug effects plus an illness.
Heroin use can also be missed, because its marker can fall after death. Levels also depend on where and when samples are taken.

item.statement: People who have used LSD or magic mushrooms report more mental health problems than people who haven't.
item.why: But the gap vanished once their other drug use and life stress were counted: 98 in 100 had also used cannabis, for one. People were asked once, so this big US survey can't show whether these drugs cause or prevent problems.

lines.short: People who had used LSD, mushrooms or mescaline reported mental health problems 2 to 3 times as often. The gap vanished once other drug use and life stress were counted.
lines.but: People were asked once, so the survey can't show whether LSD, mushrooms or mescaline cause or prevent problems.
how: 130,152 US adults answered private computer questions at home in 2001 to 2004; 21,967 had ever used LSD, mushrooms, mescaline or peyote.
At first glance, all 20 mental health measures were 2 to 3 times as common in people who had used LSD, mushrooms or mescaline.
Those who had used LSD, mushrooms or mescaline used far more other drugs: 98 in 100 had used cannabis, against 33 in 100 of others.
Once that, risk-taking, stressful events and background were counted, no measure was higher for LSD, mushrooms or mescaline. A few were lower, maybe by chance.

item.statement: People drive about as well after weed as they do sober.
item.why: Across 80 lab studies, people weaved more in their lane and reacted more slowly soon after THC than after a dummy. These are lab averages, so they can't give anyone a safe time to drive.

lines.short: For several hours; probably longer after eating it than smoking it, and longer after bigger doses.
lines.but: These are averages from lab studies, not a safe time to drive for you.
how: Researchers pooled 80 studies in which people took THC or a dummy (placebo), then did driving and attention tests.
Soon after THC, people weaved more in their lane and reacted more slowly than after the dummy.
The effects faded over several hours, probably more slowly when THC was eaten than when it was smoked or vaped.
People who use cannabis weekly or more were less affected than people who use it less often, but the study could not work out for how long.

item.statement: Most people who use kratom say they take it to get high.
item.why: In two US surveys, pain was the top reason, then anxiety or depression, and kratom's 'high' scored just 12 of 100. But the surveys reached people mostly through a pro-kratom group.

lines.short: Mostly for pain, anxiety or depression, people told two surveys, and most felt it helped. In one, about 4 in 10 had used kratom to cut down or stop opioids.
lines.but: Both surveys reached people mostly through a pro-kratom group, and those who quit after bad experiences were left out of one and may be too few in the other.
how: In 2016 and 2017, online surveys asked 8,049 and 2,798 US adults who used kratom. Most were White, working and middle-aged.
Pain was the top reason (68 and 91 in 100), then anxiety or depression. In 2017, kratom's 'good effects' scored 86 of 100, 'high' 12.
In 2017, 1,144 had used kratom to cut down or stop opioids; 849 credited it with 6 months or more off opioids. Nobody checked.
703 felt unwell after 12 to 48 hours without kratom (2016). On a checklist, 68 of 2,798 had moderate or severe kratom use disorder (2017).

item.statement: Whether someone develops a drug problem comes down to their genes, not the home they grow up in.
item.why: Both are linked. In a Swedish study of adopted children, drug problems were about twice as common when a birth parent had one, and also more common in adoptive brothers and sisters, not related by birth, when the adopted child had one.

lines.short: Both are linked: what comes from birth parents, and the home a child grows up in.
lines.but: One Swedish study. What birth parents pass on includes the pregnancy, not just genes.
how: In Sweden, 18,115 adopted children born 1950 to 1993 were followed in health, prescription and court records until 2009.
Some birth parents had a drug problem on record. Their children, raised by adoptive parents, had one about twice as often: about 9 in 100, against 4 in 100 when neither birth parent did.
Adoptive brothers and sisters are not related by birth. Still, 6 in 100 of them had a drug problem when the adopted child had one, against 3 in 100 when the child did not.

The study did not work out a share due to genes. Where studies give one, it is about differences between people in one place and time. It does not say how much of your own risk comes from genes, and it can change when living conditions change.

item.statement: Sniffing solvents or sprays has been followed by sudden death in young people.
item.why: A 1969 US survey described 110 such deaths among people aged 11 to 23; in several, the person suddenly ran or panicked before collapsing. It counted deaths only, so it can't give the risk among everyone who used these products.

lines.short: Sudden deaths after sniffing solvents and sprays were reported in one old survey.
lines.but: It counted deaths, without measuring risk among everyone who used these products.
how: A 1969 US survey described 110 deaths among young people aged 11 to 23, mostly involving sprays or a cleaning solvent. The report did not list poppers.
In several witnessed deaths, the person suddenly ran or panicked before collapsing. Where autopsies were described, they found no other cause.
The author proposed an effect on the heart's rhythm. No heart trace was recorded.
Families or friends hid the sniffing in 8 deaths, so some other deaths may have been missed.

item.statement: Misleading news stories about fentanyl harming police by touch got far more Facebook shares than the corrections did.
item.why: US news articles coded as misinformation got about 450,000 Facebook shares; clear corrections got under 30,000. In three US surveys, about 4 in 5 police and other first responders thought touching fentanyl could cause an overdose or death.

lines.short: In three US surveys, about 4 in 5 police and other first responders thought touching fentanyl could cause an overdose or death. Right after trainings, far fewer did.
lines.but: No survey picked people at random. Answers came right after training, with no untrained group or later check.
how: In Missouri, only about 1 in 5 of 140 police, paramedics and firefighters rejected the idea before training; about 5 in 6 did right after.
Officers in five US police forces said they heard it from colleagues, a federal drug agency video and bulletins; none could confirm a colleague's overdose.
506 of 551 US news articles were coded misinformation, even plain reports of ill officers. They got about 450,000 Facebook shares; clear corrections, under 30,000.

In a 2019 New York online survey, 149 of 187 police, fire and ambulance workers agreed a brief touch could be deadly. For fentanyl safety information, most named courses and training; about 1 in 7, the news.

item.statement: People who use weed several days a week are less motivated than people who have barely tried it.
item.why: In a London study, people using cannabis about 4 days a week felt no less motivated and were as willing to work for sweets. It was a one-time snapshot, so it can't show what years of heavy daily use do.

lines.short: In a London study, people using cannabis about 4 days a week felt no less motivated than people who had used it fewer than 10 times, and were as willing to work for sweets.
lines.but: A one-time snapshot of people using about 4 days a week: it can't show what cannabis does over years or with heavy daily use.
how: In London, 147 teens and adults using cannabis 1 to 7 days a week were compared with 127 who had used it under 10 times.
About half also did two tasks: pressing buttons to earn sweets, and rating how much they wanted and liked a song, chocolate and a coin.
Scores differed more by age than by cannabis use: teens reported less motivation and less pleasure than adults, whether or not they used cannabis.
It tested people at least 12 hours after their last cannabis, with questionnaires and lab tasks, not school or work; small differences could be missed.

item.statement: Teenagers in London reported less motivation than adults, whether or not they used weed.
item.why: Scores differed more by age than by cannabis use: teens reported less motivation and less pleasure than adults either way. People were tested with questionnaires and lab tasks, not at school or work.

lines.short: In a London study, people using cannabis about 4 days a week felt no less motivated than people who had used it fewer than 10 times, and were as willing to work for sweets.
lines.but: A one-time snapshot of people using about 4 days a week: it can't show what cannabis does over years or with heavy daily use.
how: In London, 147 teens and adults using cannabis 1 to 7 days a week were compared with 127 who had used it under 10 times.
About half also did two tasks: pressing buttons to earn sweets, and rating how much they wanted and liked a song, chocolate and a coin.
Scores differed more by age than by cannabis use: teens reported less motivation and less pleasure than adults, whether or not they used cannabis.
It tested people at least 12 hours after their last cannabis, with questionnaires and lab tasks, not school or work; small differences could be missed.

item.statement: When people stop long-term heavy drinking, their sleep is back to normal within a few days.
item.why: In sleep-lab studies, many slept badly for weeks or months after stopping, with less deep sleep. This comes second-hand from one review that did not check how good the studies were.

lines.short: Alcohol can help people fall asleep at first, but studies in one review found long heavy drinking leaves sleep poor for months.
lines.but: This comes second-hand from a review that did not check how good the studies were.
how: Sleep labs compared people who had drunk heavily for a long time with good sleepers.
Many slept badly while drinking and for weeks or months after stopping, with less deep sleep.
In several studies, people who said they slept badly soon after stopping were more likely to drink again than those who did not.

item.statement: People off cocaine for several months scored close to people who don't use it on memory and attention tests.
item.why: In 5 studies of people who had stopped for more than about 5 months, scores were close to the comparison groups. But these were other people, not the same people tested again.

lines.short: On average, people with cocaine problems score somewhat lower on memory and attention tests.
lines.but: No one was tested before they started, so we can't tell if cocaine caused the gap.
how: Five reviews pulled together small studies that compared people with cocaine problems with people who don't use cocaine.
Most gaps were small to medium, and studies disagree about the size. The newest review got the numbers of two small studies wrong, which made its gap look bigger.
Many also drank or used other drugs, some were tested within three days of last use, and most studies did not check scores against the normal range.
In 5 studies of people who had stopped for more than about 5 months, scores were close to the comparison groups. But these were other people, not the same people tested again.

item.statement: Before it was banned in 1985, MDMA was used by some US therapists in talking therapy.
item.why: A few dozen US therapists used it and reported good results, but the reports of the time were not designed well enough to show whether it helped. After the ban, research applications were blocked for years.

lines.short: Before MDMA was banned in 1985, a few dozen US therapists used it in talking therapy.
lines.but: This comes second-hand from one history review, and the reports of the time were not designed well enough to show whether MDMA helped.
how: Therapists reported good results, and a follow-up of 29 patients found no serious side effects.
Two therapists had sexual contact with patients during sessions and lost their licences.
A US judge said the strictest ban was not needed, but the drug agency imposed it anyway.
Research applications were then blocked for years; the first approved study, in healthy people, began in 1992.

item.statement: Drinking beer before wine gives a milder hangover than wine before beer.
item.why: When young adults drank beer and wine in both orders on different days, the hangover was about the same. Only one kind of beer and one white wine were tested.

lines.short: Drinking beer before wine or wine before beer gave about the same hangover.
lines.but: Only one kind of beer and one white wine were tested.
how: Young adults drank beer and wine on two days, in a different order each time.
Doctors watched them, and they slept at the university.
Each person's hangover after one order was compared with their hangover after the other order.

item.statement: In their first weeks off cocaine, people felt they slept better while sleep-lab machines showed them sleeping worse.
item.why: By the third week, machines showed they took longer to fall asleep and slept less, yet their own ratings of sleep got better. It's one small study of 20 people in a hospital unit.

lines.short: Over three weeks off cocaine, measured sleep got worse while people felt they slept better.
lines.but: One small study of 20 people in a hospital unit; daytime light and withdrawal from other drugs were not controlled.
how: Twenty people with cocaine dependence slept in a sleep lab during their first weeks off cocaine.
Machines showed they took longer to fall asleep and slept less by the third week.
Dreaming (REM) sleep went down, while deep sleep went up a little.
Their own ratings of sleep got better, and were no worse than healthy men's.

item.statement: Most people who have had a drinking problem have not looked for treatment or help.
item.why: In a US survey, about 20 in 100 people who had ever had alcohol use disorder said they had looked for help, and about 35 in 100 of those with a severe one. People reported this themselves, and the survey left out most people in treatment.

lines.short: In a US survey, 20 in 100 people who ever had it sought help.
lines.but: People said this themselves, and the survey left out most people who were in treatment.
how: In 2012 and 2013, a US survey asked people with alcohol use disorder whether they had ever looked for treatment or help.
About 20 in 100 who had ever had it said yes, and about 8 in 100 of those who had it in the past year.
Groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous were the most common kind of help. People with severe disorder looked for help more often: about 35 in 100, against 4 in 100 with mild disorder.
A review passes on about 22 in 100 for Europe and the world, but these count people who got treatment, not people who looked for it.

item.statement: When weed use in the UK soared after the 1970s, hospital stays for schizophrenia climbed with it.
item.why: A review says cannabis use rose at least tenfold while first hospital stays for schizophrenia did not rise. But studies disagree: psychosis did become more common in people born more recently in south-east London and Zurich.

lines.short: Studies disagree: some places saw more psychosis over time, others no rise as use grew.
lines.but: We know these studies only through reviews, and changes in diagnosis can blur trends.
how: In Australia, a study found no clear rise in psychosis after cannabis use went up in the 1980s and 1990s.
In south-east London and in Zurich, psychosis became more common in people born more recently.
A review says that in the UK cannabis use rose at least tenfold since the 1970s, while first hospital stays for schizophrenia did not rise.
Even if cannabis played a part, the rise would be small and hard to see in health records.

item.statement: In one study, older people who took the most benzos got dementia about as often as those who took none.
item.why: About 3 in 100 a year got dementia either way, in a Seattle study that tested 3,434 older people. Quebec health records did link long use to Alzheimer's, but early dementia can bring the worry and poor sleep that lead to the pills.

lines.short: Not known. In Quebec health records, long use of benzodiazepines was linked to Alzheimer's. A Seattle study that tested people found no clear link with the heaviest use.
lines.but: Neither study could rule out that early dementia, which can bring worry and poor sleep, led to the prescriptions.
how: In Quebec records, 50 in 100 older people with Alzheimer's had filled benzodiazepine prescriptions 5 to 10 years before, against 40 in 100 without it.
The link appeared only with longer use. The records often missed why the pills were taken, and held nothing on education, smoking or drinking.
A Seattle study tested 3,434 older people every 2 years. About 3 in 100 a year got dementia, with the heaviest use or none.
A small extra risk showed up with light or moderate use, not the heaviest. The authors say early dementia symptoms may explain it.

item.statement: After Vancouver opened a supervised injection site, overdose deaths in the streets around it went up.
item.why: Within 500 metres they fell by about a third, against about a tenth elsewhere in the city. It's one site, before and after, and nothing else was ruled out, so this doesn't prove the site was the reason.

lines.short: Not proven: near Vancouver's site for injecting heroin, cocaine and other drugs, overdose deaths fell about a third after it opened. Elsewhere in the city, about a tenth.
lines.but: Just one site, before and after, and nothing else was ruled out, such as extra police.
how: Coroners recorded 290 overdose deaths from illegal drugs in Vancouver, 2001 to 2005. About half involved opioids, and about 6 in 10 cocaine.
Within 500 metres: 56 deaths in the 2.7 years before it opened in 2003, 33 in the 2.3 after, about 6 fewer a year.
Critics blamed extra police from April 2003. The authors said that crackdown ended within weeks of the opening.
Critics also blamed the study's start in 2001, a year with more heroin around. The two papers they cited show overdoses falling since the late 1990s, but neither measured heroin's strength or price.

item.statement: When an antidepressant dulls MDMA's effects, there is also less MDMA in your blood.
item.why: In small trials, two antidepressants lowered how strongly people rated MDMA's effects, yet the MDMA peak in their blood was about 15 to 18 percent higher. That's second-hand, from single trials of 16 healthy people each.

lines.short: Other antidepressants did not act alike: some muted MDMA's effects, and bupropion did not.
lines.but: These numbers are second-hand, from a 2022 review of single trials with 16 healthy people each.
how: Duloxetine and reboxetine lowered MDMA's rated effects. The MDMA peak in the blood was about 15 to 18 percent higher.
Bupropion did not lower the ratings. The MDMA level was higher too (about 14 percent at the peak, 33 percent over the day), while heart rate rose less.

Some people feel little from an amount and take more. A slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, bodies that differ or a muting medicine can each be the reason. No trial tested what happened then.
The review's authors guess, without data, that bupropion with MDMA might raise the chance of seizures.

item.statement: In lab driving tests, people did just as well soon after THC, cannabis's main active part, as after a dummy version.
item.why: In 80 pooled lab studies, people weaved more in their lane and reacted more slowly than after a dummy.

lines.short: For several hours; probably longer after eating it than smoking it, and longer after bigger doses.
lines.but: These are averages from lab studies, not a safe time to drive for you.
how: Researchers pooled 80 studies in which people took THC or a dummy (placebo), then did driving and attention tests.
Soon after THC, people weaved more in their lane and reacted more slowly than after the dummy.
The effects faded over several hours, probably more slowly when THC was eaten than when it was smoked or vaped.
People who use cannabis weekly or more were less affected than people who use it less often, but the study could not work out for how long.

item.why: In 80 pooled lab studies, people weaved more in their lane and reacted more slowly than after a dummy.

lines.short: For several hours; probably longer after eating it than smoking it, and longer after bigger doses.
lines.but: These are averages from lab studies, not a safe time to drive for you.

item.statement: Taking benzos such as Xanax or Valium for a long time has been shown to cause dementia.
item.why: Not shown: neither of two studies could rule out that early dementia, which can bring worry and poor sleep, led to the prescriptions. Quebec records linked long use to Alzheimer's, but a Seattle study that tested people found no clear link with the heaviest use.

lines.short: Not known. In Quebec health records, long use of benzodiazepines was linked to Alzheimer's. A Seattle study that tested people found no clear link with the heaviest use.
lines.but: Neither study could rule out that early dementia, which can bring worry and poor sleep, led to the prescriptions.
how: In Quebec records, 50 in 100 older people with Alzheimer's had filled benzodiazepine prescriptions 5 to 10 years before, against 40 in 100 without it.
The link appeared only with longer use. The records often missed why the pills were taken, and held nothing on education, smoking or drinking.
A Seattle study tested 3,434 older people every 2 years. About 3 in 100 a year got dementia, with the heaviest use or none.
A small extra risk showed up with light or moderate use, not the heaviest. The authors say early dementia symptoms may explain it.

item.statement: In a lab test, people rated trips on LSD and on psilocybin, the drug in magic mushrooms, as much alike.
item.why: In 28 people, the ratings barely differed. But that's no proof they're the same, and most could tell which drug they'd had.

lines.short: Mostly how long it lasts: about 9 to 11 hours for LSD, 6 to 7 for psilocybin, the drug in mushrooms. Otherwise 28 lab volunteers rated the trips alike on most measures.
lines.but: Finding no difference in 28 people doesn't prove there is none. And most could tell which drug they'd had.
how: 28 healthy adults each had five hospital days, at least 10 days apart. They got a dummy, two amounts of LSD and two of psilocybin, in random order, not told which.
LSD lasted longer at both amounts. It also began a bit sooner, which the authors put down to it being a liquid, not a capsule.
The higher psilocybin amount raised blood pressure and body temperature a little more. LSD raised heart rate more. Both brought complaints like headaches; nobody had a serious problem.
By the study's own figures, people named the right drug in most sessions, which may have shaped their ratings. It used pure psilocybin in capsules, not mushrooms.

item.statement: In a lab study, caffeine made people with a caffeine habit more alert than people who rarely have it.
item.why: Caffeine only brought them up to the alertness of people who rarely have it. One study; people chose their own habits.

lines.short: In one lab study, caffeine made everyone faster. But those who often have it only got as alert as those who rarely do.
lines.but: Only one study, and people chose their own caffeine habits, so something else about them could explain it.
how: In Bristol, UK, 416 adults were asked to skip caffeine overnight. The next day, chance decided who got caffeine pills and who got dummy pills.
By the afternoon, people who often have caffeine but got dummy pills were the sleepiest and slowest. They made the most mistakes.
Caffeine brought them about level with people who rarely have it, no higher. In those people, caffeine raised jitters, not alertness.
Five people who often have caffeine quit the test day early. All five had dummy pills; four gave headache and feeling sick as reasons.

item.statement: In 2001 Portugal made it no longer a crime to have any drug for your own use. After that, drug use fell.
item.why: It rose slightly, from about 8 to 12 in 100 adults ever trying one. Treatment grew too, so the law's effect is unclear.

lines.short: Mixed. Adults who'd ever tried a drug went from 8 to 12 in 100, but use in the last year barely moved. New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell.
lines.but: Treatment and other help grew too, starting in 1999, so these figures can't show what the law alone did.
how: In 2001, having any drug for your own use became an offence handled by regional panels, not a crime. Mostly for that reason, crime arrests for drugs fell from over 14,000 to 5,000–5,500 a year.
Adults who had ever tried an illegal drug rose from about 8 to 12 in 100 (2001 to 2007); past-year use barely changed.
New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell from 907 (2000) to 267 (2008). The paper says this has been credited mainly to more harm reduction services, without saying by whom.
Deaths doctors judged drug-caused fell from about 76 to 20 (2001 to 2008). Deaths with drugs found fell, then rose as testing more than doubled.

item.statement: In studies, people who had been off cocaine for more than about 5 months still scored clearly lower on memory tests.
item.why: Their scores were close to the comparison groups. But these were other people, not the same people tested again.

lines.short: On average, people with cocaine problems score somewhat lower on memory and attention tests.
lines.but: No one was tested before they started, so we can't tell if cocaine caused the gap.
how: Five reviews pulled together small studies that compared people with cocaine problems with people who don't use cocaine.
Most gaps were small to medium, and studies disagree about the size. The newest review got the numbers of two small studies wrong, which made its gap look bigger.
Many also drank or used other drugs, some were tested within three days of last use, and most studies did not check scores against the normal range.
In 5 studies of people who had stopped for more than about 5 months, scores were close to the comparison groups. But these were other people, not the same people tested again.

item.statement: In a US survey, people who used LSD or mushrooms had more mental health problems, even after counting their other differences.
item.why: Before counting, problems were about 2 to 3 times as common; after counting other drugs, risk-taking and stressful events, none of 20 was higher.

lines.short: People who had used LSD, mushrooms or mescaline reported mental health problems 2 to 3 times as often. The gap vanished once other drug use and life stress were counted.
lines.but: People were asked once, so the survey can't show whether LSD, mushrooms or mescaline cause or prevent problems.
how: 130,152 US adults answered private computer questions at home in 2001 to 2004; 21,967 had ever used LSD, mushrooms, mescaline or peyote.
At first glance, all 20 mental health measures were 2 to 3 times as common in people who had used LSD, mushrooms or mescaline.
Those who had used LSD, mushrooms or mescaline used far more other drugs: 98 in 100 had used cannabis, against 33 in 100 of others.
Once that, risk-taking, stressful events and background were counted, no measure was higher for LSD, mushrooms or mescaline. A few were lower, maybe by chance.
